note: Prompt 08 knowledge questions. Each has 3 answers, the right one (index from 0), a plain explanation tied to the colony's equipment, and at least one retry variant (changed numbers or situation). Answering right records state.knowledge[id] once. role: guided (tier 1 explanation check), diagnosis (tier 2: shown in a changed example, never the guided one's), transfer (tier 3), check (card question). 'example' names the situation, so the game can tell a changed example from the guided one. Numbers in questions are the game's model values (game balance) unless a source id is named.

questions.title: Why dusty panels give less power

variants.text: At noon the 12 panels give 55 kW. On a clear day with clean panels they gave 100 kW. The sky is normal and the trackers turn. What is the most likely cause?
answers: Dust has settled on the panels and blocks the sunlight
The colony uses too many lights
variants.explanation: Settled dust covers part of each panel, so less sunlight reaches it. Panels 45 % covered give about 45 % less power. Cleaning them at the trackers, or repairing the panel cleaner, brings the power back.

variants.text: Tracker 4 gives 4 kW at noon. The trackers next to it give 8 kW each. They all turn to face the sun. What is wrong with tracker 4?
answers: Its panel is covered in dust
It is too far from the battery
variants.explanation: All trackers see the same sun and sky, so a panel that gives half as much has something on it: dust. Cleaning that one panel fixes it.

questions.title: Find the cause of a power loss in a new case

variants.text: The panels give 60 kW at noon instead of 100 kW. The sky is clear and the trackers turn. Which check comes first?
answers: Look at the dust on the panels
variants.explanation: With a clear sky and turning trackers, the usual cause is dust on the panels. Check the dust first; then clean the panels or repair the cleaner.

variants.text: All 12 panels were cleaned this morning, but at noon they give only 60 kW. The sky is dark orange with dust in the air. What is the cause?
answers: Dust in the air blocks sunlight before it reaches the panels
variants.explanation: Clean panels still get less sun when a dust storm fills the air. Cleaning will not help: save power until the sky clears.

variants.text: The panels are clean and the sky is clear, but power is lower than usual and the panels point straight up all day. What is the cause?
answers: The sun trackers have stopped turning the panels
variants.explanation: Trackers turn the panels to face the sun. When they stop (switched off, broken or shed for lack of power), fixed panels catch the sun at a slant and make less power.

questions.title: Predict the battery from the readings

variants.text: Look at the power panel. Suppose the sun gives 30 kW and the colony asks for 42 kW. What does the battery do?
answers: It gives 12 kW to cover the gap
variants.explanation: Power in minus power asked for: 30 − 42 = −12 kW. The battery gives the missing 12 kW, so the kWh stored in it go down.

variants.text: Look at the power panel. Suppose the sun gives 50 kW and the colony asks for 38 kW. What does the battery do?
answers: It charges with the 12 kW left over
variants.explanation: 50 − 38 = +12 kW left over. The battery stores it (about a tenth is lost as heat while charging).

questions.title: Why a solar colony needs a battery

variants.text: Why does a colony that runs on sunlight need a battery?
answers: At night the panels make no power, but the air machines must keep running
variants.explanation: The panels give nothing between sunset and sunrise. The CO2 scrubber, the fans and the heating run all night on the energy the battery stored during the day.

variants.text: It is 03:00 at night. What keeps the CO2 scrubber running?
variants.explanation: At night there is no sunlight, so every machine that runs is powered from the battery.

variants.text: Why does a panel on a sun tracker give more power over a sol than a fixed panel?
answers: It is closer to the sun
It faces the sun all day, so sunlight hits it straight on
It stores sunlight for the night
variants.explanation: Light that hits a panel straight on gives the most power. A tracker keeps turning the panel to face the sun, so it catches more light in the morning and the evening.

variants.text: In the morning the sun is low in the east. A fixed panel points straight up. A tracker panel turns east. Which gives more power?
variants.explanation: The tracker panel faces the low sun, the fixed panel gets the light at a slant. The tracker wins, most of all early and late in the sol.

variants.text: The panel cleaner is broken and nobody repairs it. What happens over the next sols?
answers: Power slowly falls as dust builds up
variants.explanation: A little dust settles on the panels every sol. Without the cleaner wiping them at sunrise, it builds up and the panels give less and less power.

variants.text: The cleaner works, but at sunrise it has no power because the battery is empty. What happens?
answers: The dust stays until the cleaner has power at a sunrise
variants.explanation: The cleaner only wipes the panels when it is on, working and powered at sunrise. Keeping a little battery for the morning matters.

variants.text: A dust storm will darken the sky for several sols. Panels give less power even when clean. What is the best plan?
answers: Switch off rooms and machines that are not needed, so the battery lasts
Switch everything on to use the power while it lasts
variants.explanation: During a storm less sunlight reaches the panels, so less energy comes in. Use less: switch off lights and machines nobody needs, and keep the battery for life support.

variants.text: During a storm the panels give 40 kW at noon instead of 100 kW. The colony asks for 45 kW all day. What does the battery do at noon?
answers: It gives 5 kW even at noon
variants.explanation: 40 − 45 = −5 kW: even at noon the sun is not enough, so the battery keeps going down. Switch off 5 kW or more of loads.

variants.text: The colony has two oxygen makers: the electrolyser and the CO2-oxygen unit. Which one needs water?
variants.explanation: The electrolyser splits water into hydrogen and oxygen (about 1.1 L of water per kg of oxygen), like on the ISS (S08). The CO2-oxygen unit takes carbon dioxide from the Mars air and uses only power, like MOXIE (S09).

variants.text: Clean water is low, but there is plenty of power. Which oxygen maker can still run without taking water?
variants.explanation: The CO2-oxygen unit uses the carbon dioxide in the Mars air and power, no water. The electrolyser needs feed water.

questions.title: Fix an oxygen problem in a new case

variants.text: The electrolyser is switched on but makes no oxygen. The console says 'no feed water'. What do you do?
answers: Send water to it with the water allocation
variants.explanation: The electrolyser needs feed water. Set the electrolyser water allocation at the life-support console (drinking water always comes first).

variants.text: The electrolyser stopped: 'water not clean enough'. The water recycler is in poor condition. What is a good plan?
answers: Switch the electrolyser off and on again
Run the CO2-oxygen unit meanwhile and get the recycler working well so the water becomes clean
variants.explanation: The cause is the water quality, which comes from the recycler. The CO2-oxygen unit needs no water, so it can make oxygen while the water gets clean again.

variants.text: At night the battery is low and both oxygen makers stopped with 'no power'. The oxygen reserve has 50 kg and falls about 3 kg per sol. What is the right call?
answers: The cabin air runs out tonight
The reserve covers many sols: switch off lights so the battery lasts, and the makers restart when the sun is up
variants.explanation: The tanks are a store: 50 kg at 3 kg per sol lasts many sols. Save power for the scrubber and fans tonight.

variants.text: The oxygen reserve fell from 60 kg to 50 kg, but the cabin oxygen is still 21 kPa. Why?
answers: The regulator tops up the cabin air from the tanks, so the tanks fall first
The cabin leaks oxygen into the tanks
variants.explanation: The oxygen reserve (kg in tanks) is a store. The cabin oxygen (kPa) is the air you breathe. The regulator keeps the cabin at 21 kPa by taking oxygen from the tanks.

variants.text: The oxygen tanks are empty. What happens to the cabin oxygen pressure?
answers: It jumps to zero at once
It slowly falls as the crew breathes, because nothing tops it up
variants.explanation: The cabin still holds its air. With nothing to top it up, every breath takes a little oxygen out, so the pressure falls slowly. Start an oxygen maker.

variants.text: Cabin CO2 is rising. The CO2 scrubber is on, but the cabin fans are off. Why?
answers: The fans move air through the scrubber; without them it cleans only part of the air
variants.explanation: The scrubber can only clean the air that reaches it. The fans push the cabin air through it; without them it removes only about a quarter as much.

variants.text: Four crew are inside instead of two. What happens to the CO2 they breathe out each hour?
answers: It doubles, so the scrubber has twice as much to remove
variants.explanation: Each person breathes out about the same amount of CO2. Twice the people, twice the CO2.

variants.text: The water recycler gets 10 L of wastewater. About 90 % comes back clean. How much clean water is that?
variants.explanation: 90 % of 10 L is 9 L. The ISS recovers about 90 percent of its water (S08); the last litre is left as brine.

variants.text: The recycler gets 20 L of wastewater and returns 90 % of it clean. How much is left as brine?
variants.explanation: 90 % of 20 L = 18 L comes back clean; the other 10 %, 2 L, is brine.

variants.text: Making 1 kg of oxygen by electrolysis uses about how much water?
variants.explanation: 2 H2O → 2 H2 + O2: 36 g of water gives 32 g of oxygen, so 1 kg of oxygen needs about 1.13 kg (1.1 L) of water. That is chemistry, not a game number.

variants.text: The electrolyser made 2 kg of oxygen today. About how much water did it use?
variants.explanation: About 1.13 L per kg, so 2 kg uses about 2.3 L. The hydrogen that is left over is vented.

variants.text: Where does the CO2-oxygen unit get its oxygen from?
answers: From the carbon dioxide in the Mars air
variants.explanation: It takes one oxygen atom from each CO2 molecule of the Mars air. MOXIE did this on Mars, best 12 g per hour (S09). Our colony-size unit is fiction scaled up from it.

variants.text: The CO2-oxygen unit takes one oxygen atom from each CO2 molecule. What is left over?
answers: Carbon monoxide, which is vented outside
variants.explanation: CO2 minus one O is CO, carbon monoxide. It is poisonous, so the unit vents it outside.

variants.text: Two more crew members start working, so four breathe instead of two. Which reserve must you watch more closely?
answers: The oxygen reserve: it now falls about twice as fast
variants.explanation: Each person breathes about the same. Twice the crew uses oxygen twice as fast, so the reserve falls faster unless the oxygen makers run more.

variants.text: The scrubber removes up to 0.4 kg of CO2 per hour. Each crew member breathes out about 0.04 kg per hour. With 4 crew inside, is the scrubber big enough?
answers: No, it is far too small
Yes: 4 × 0.04 = 0.16 kg per hour, less than 0.4
Only if the fans are off
variants.explanation: 4 × 0.04 = 0.16 kg per hour, well under 0.4. It is big enough while the fans run (without fans it gets only part of the air).

variants.text: Lettuce leaves turn yellow. The light is on, the water is fine, and the nutrient reading is 0.2 (low). What is the cause?
variants.explanation: Yellow leaves with a low nutrient reading point to missing nutrients. The measurement proves it: light and water are fine.

variants.text: Tomato plants droop and wilt. The light is on, nutrients read 0.7, and the bed's water reads 0.05 (nearly dry). What is the cause?
variants.explanation: Wilting with a nearly dry water reading means the roots get too little water. Check the greenhouse water allocation.

questions.title: Find a plant problem in a new case

variants.text: A different bed shows yellow leaves. Before changing anything, what do you check?
answers: The measured nutrient level of that bed
variants.explanation: A symptom is a clue, the measurement is the proof. Read that bed's nutrient level before you change it.

variants.text: Lettuce grows tall, thin and pale. Water reads 0.8 and nutrients 0.7, but the Greenhouse lights were shed during a night of low power. What is the cause?
variants.explanation: Tall, thin, pale plants are stretching for light. Water and nutrients are fine, so the cause is the missing light.

variants.text: Plants wilt after someone set the greenhouse water allocation to 0 L per hour. Light and nutrients are fine. What is the cause?
answers: No water reaches the beds: the allocation is 0
variants.explanation: The beds only get the water the allocation sends. With 0 L per hour they slowly dry out.

questions.title: Change one thing at a time

variants.text: A bed has yellow leaves. Why change only the nutrients, and not also the light and water at the same time?
answers: So you can tell which change helped
variants.explanation: If you change one input and the plants recover, you know that input was the cause. Change three at once and you cannot tell.

variants.text: Sam raised the nutrients AND the water on a wilting bed, and it got better. What do we know?
answers: We cannot tell which change helped
variants.explanation: Two changes at once hide the cause. Next time, change one input and watch the growth.

variants.text: Where does the water for the greenhouse beds come from?
answers: From the clean water store, through the greenhouse water allocation
variants.explanation: The life-support console sends clean water to the greenhouse at the allocated litres per hour. Used water goes to the wastewater tank and the recycler.

variants.text: The greenhouse allocation is 2 L per hour, but clean water is below the 100 L drinking reserve. How much reaches the beds?
variants.explanation: Allocations only take water above the drinking reserve. Below it, nothing goes to the greenhouse until the store rises.

variants.text: Power runs short and the Greenhouse lights are shed. What happens to the plants?
answers: Growth slows or stops until the light is back
variants.explanation: Plants use light to grow. Without it, growth slows or stops; it starts again when the lights come back.

variants.text: Why do the greenhouse lights use much more power (9 kW) than the room lights?
answers: Plants need much more light than people to grow
variants.explanation: People only need light to see; plants need a lot of light to grow. That is why greenhouse lights are a big load.

questions.title: Use what you learned on another crop

variants.text: You learned to fix low nutrients in lettuce. Now tomatoes show yellow leaves and read 0.2 nutrients. What do you try first?
answers: Raise the nutrients of the tomato bed and watch its growth
variants.explanation: Same symptom, same measurement, different crop: try the same single change and check the growth rate rises.

variants.text: Lettuce has grown on the ISS in Veggie; tomato is only a plan there so far. What does our greenhouse tell us about farming on Mars?
answers: It is a game model based on ISS tests; it does not prove farming on Mars
variants.explanation: The ISS grew lettuce (S11); tomatoes were planned (S11, S13). Our greenhouse is a model built on that, sped up for the game. It does not prove Mars agriculture.

variants.text: The water recycler needs a pump with a 40 mm port and a 24 V motor. The old filter unit has a 40 mm 24 V pump, a 60 mm valve and a 12 V fan. Which part fits?
variants.explanation: A compatible part matches what the machine needs: the same type, size and voltage. Only the 40 mm 24 V pump matches.

variants.text: The battery rack needs cells of the same type and voltage as the others (lithium, 3.6 V). A damaged rack has 3.6 V lithium cells, 12 V lead cells and a cooling fan. Which is compatible?
variants.explanation: Cells must match the others in type and voltage. Mixing cell types or voltages in one rack is unsafe.

questions.title: Judge a salvaged part in a new case

variants.text: A pump fits the 40 mm port, but its motor is 12 V and the colony line is 24 V. Use it?
answers: No: the voltage does not match, so it would not work safely
variants.explanation: Fitting one measurement is not enough. Every match must hold: type, size and voltage.

variants.text: A salvaged valve has the right size and voltage, but its housing is cracked. What do you do?
answers: Do not use it until it is refurbished and passes a bench test
variants.explanation: A damaged part can fail in the machine. Refurbish it at the workbench and bench-test it first.

variants.text: A part from the crash site has no label. What is the safe first step?
answers: Measure its size and voltage and compare them with what the machine needs
variants.explanation: Without a label, measure. Then compare with the machine's needs before you recover or refurbish it.

variants.text: Why bench-test a refurbished part before it goes into the colony?
answers: To find faults safely before a machine depends on it
variants.explanation: A bench test runs the part on the workbench, where a fault does no harm. A fault found inside the water recycler would.

variants.text: A refurbished pump fails its bench test. What did the test save you from?
answers: Installing a broken pump in the water recycler
variants.explanation: The test caught the fault before the colony relied on the pump.

variants.text: Can the workbench turn a rock into a new circuit board?
answers: No: a component comes from real parts; the bench repairs and refits them
variants.explanation: The workbench cannot make electronics from rock. It turns a salvaged part into a working one: one part in, one component out.

variants.text: You refurbish one salvaged pump. How many working pumps do you get?
answers: One: the salvaged pump becomes the working one
variants.explanation: Refurbishing repairs the part you brought. Nothing is created from nothing.

variants.text: A new wreck is found with many parts. How do you choose what to recover?
answers: Check what the colony's machines need (type, size, voltage) and recover only compatible parts
variants.explanation: Carrying space and time are limited. Recover what matches a real need.

variants.text: A donor part matches but lay outside through dust storms for years. What changes in your plan?
answers: Inspect it for dust and wear, refurbish it and bench-test it before use
variants.explanation: New conditions (dust, cold, years outside) mean more wear. The same steps keep it safe: inspect, refurbish, test.

variants.text: Why write down the site, the time and the conditions when you take a field sample?
answers: So later results can be compared and checked
variants.explanation: A result only means something if you know where and when the sample came from. The notes let anyone compare and repeat it.

variants.text: Two samples look the same, but one was taken near the crash site just after a dust storm. Why does the note matter?
answers: Dust from the storm or the crash could change the result, so we need to know
variants.explanation: Conditions can change what a sample contains. The note tells you which results can fairly be compared.

questions.title: Read an odd result in a new case

variants.text: A sample result looks odd. What do you look at first?
answers: The notes: site, time and conditions when it was taken
variants.explanation: Start with the context: an odd site or condition often explains an odd result.

variants.text: The blank control (a test that should show nothing) shows a signal. What does that tell you?
answers: Something in the lab is contaminating the test; fix that before trusting results
variants.explanation: A control that shows a signal means the test itself adds something. Clean up and repeat before believing the sample.

variants.text: Your sample matches neither the reference nor the control. What is a fair next step?
answers: Repeat the test and take another sample before deciding
Say it proves life on Mars
variants.explanation: One strange result is a question, not an answer. Repeat it and gather more samples.

variants.text: In the lab you test your sample, a reference sample and a blank control. Why the blank?
answers: To check the instrument shows nothing when there is nothing
variants.explanation: The blank shows what the instrument reads with no sample. Anything above that comes from the sample.

variants.text: The blank control reads zero and the reference reads its known value. What does that mean for your sample's result?
answers: You can trust the instrument more
variants.explanation: The instrument passed both checks, so its reading of your sample is more trustworthy.

variants.text: The lab's reference is linked to NASA's Curiosity rover (CheMin instrument, Gale crater). Is it a measurement of rocks at our colony?
answers: No: it is another place on Mars; we only compare with it, and its numbers here are illustrative
variants.explanation: Gale crater is a real place far from our fictional colony (S06). The game uses the mission and instrument as provenance; any mineral numbers shown are illustrative, not from the archive.

variants.text: Why compare with a well-known reference sample?
answers: To check the instrument reads known material correctly
variants.explanation: If the instrument gets the reference right, you can trust its reading of the new sample more.

variants.text: Result A is 0.6 ± 0.2. Result B is 0.6 ± 0.05. Which one tells you more precisely what the value is?
variants.explanation: The ± is the uncertainty. B says the value is between 0.55 and 0.65; A only says between 0.4 and 0.8.

variants.text: A nutrient setting from the lab is 0.5 ± 0.3. Is it safe to rely on exactly 0.5?
answers: Not very: the true value could be from 0.2 to 0.8; a calibrated instrument would narrow it
variants.explanation: A big uncertainty means a wide range. Calibration makes the range smaller, so the setting is more reliable.

questions.title: Check a lab result in the real colony

variants.text: The lab says this soil needs more nutrients for lettuce. How do you check the setting works?
answers: Apply it to one bed and compare its growth with a bed left as before
Apply it everywhere and forget it
variants.explanation: A fair comparison: one bed with the new setting, one without, everything else the same.

variants.text: A result from a dusty site is applied to a bed using clean-site soil. What should you watch?
answers: Whether that bed responds as expected, because the sites may differ
variants.explanation: New conditions can change the answer. Watch the bed's growth to check the result transfers.

questions.title: Why the colony radio is slow

variants.text: Ana is outside and says "I found the crash site!". Inside, Ben hears it 30 seconds later. What makes the wait?
answers: The damaged radio stores and cleans up her words before it sends them
Her words travel to Earth and back
The base's computer network is slow
variants.explanation: The colony radio is damaged: it has to buffer and process speech before it sends it. That equipment wait is the delay. It is not the computer network, and Earth is not involved at all.

variants.text: After a radio repair, speech from outside arrives after 15 s instead of 30 s. What did the repair change?
answers: How long the radio holds and processes speech
How fast sound moves in the air
variants.explanation: A better buffer and processor hold your words for a shorter time. The distance to Earth did not change, and outside there is almost no air to carry sound anyway.

questions.title: Radio check at the comms console

variants.text: The comms console shows: speech delay 30 s. Cara is outside and asks "Can I come in?" at 10:00:00. When does the base hear her question?
variants.explanation: The radio holds speech for 30 s, so a question asked at 10:00:00 is heard at 10:00:30, and the answer needs another 30 s to reach Cara. Keep radio messages short and clear.

variants.text: The comms console shows a 15 s speech delay. Dan outside asks a question and the base answers at once. How long after asking does Dan hear the answer?
variants.explanation: 15 s for the question to come in plus 15 s for the answer to go out: about 30 s in total. That is why radio talk needs patience until the radio is repaired.

questions.title: Why messages from Earth stay slow

variants.text: The colony radio is repaired to stage 2. Will messages from Earth now arrive faster?
answers: No: Earth messages take minutes because Earth is so far away, and the colony radio cannot change that
variants.explanation: Radio waves travel at the speed of light, but Earth is so far away that a message still needs many minutes, depending on where the planets are. The colony radio's own wait is a different thing.

variants.text: Which wait does a colony radio repair make shorter?
answers: The time a message takes to cross space to Earth
The time the colony radio holds speech while it processes it
variants.explanation: The repair fixes the colony's own equipment. The trip to Earth is set by the distance and the speed of light, so it stays the same.

variants.text: Ana and Ben are both inside the base, 3 m apart in the mess hall. How does Ben hear Ana?
answers: Over the radio, after the delay
Directly and at once, like normal talking
variants.explanation: Inside, the air carries her voice: people near her hear her at once. The radio is only used when someone is outside.

variants.text: Ana is outside by the solar panels. Ben is inside in the command room. How does Ben hear Ana?
answers: He cannot hear her even with a working radio
Over the radio, after the radio's delay
variants.explanation: Outside there is almost no air to carry sound, so suits use the radio. When either person is outside, speech goes over the radio and arrives after its delay.

variants.text: The radio delay is 5 s. Cara outside needs to know whether the airlock is ready. What is the best way to ask?
answers: One short, clear question, then wait for the answer
variants.explanation: With a delay, talking over each other makes a mess. Say one clear thing, then wait at least twice the delay for the answer.

variants.text: Dan asks a question over a radio with a 15 s delay and hears nothing for 10 s. What should he do?
answers: Wait: the answer needs about 30 s to come back
variants.explanation: 15 s for his question to arrive plus 15 s for the answer: about 30 s. Repeating too early only adds more messages waiting in the radio.
